claims.text: Greater atomic-level compositional uniformity in HEA nanoparticles causes surface premelting to begin at a lower temperature.
Compositional uniformity creates locally destabilized bonding environments through enhanced configurational entropy.
Local compositional heterogeneity reinforces surface interatomic cohesion and delays premelting.
The initial HEA nanoparticles have a random distribution of multiple principal elements.
A random elemental distribution constitutes atomic-scale configurational heterogeneity.
Processing conditions can be adjusted to produce local compositional clustering while retaining a controlled comparison with near-ideal random mixing.
Atomic-level compositional uniformity affects local cohesion and atomic-size-mismatch environments.
Uniformly mixed nanoparticles have higher configurational entropy than locally clustered nanoparticles.
Higher configurational entropy weakens localized surface bonding.
Weaker localized surface bonding lowers the local melting threshold and triggers premelting.
Local compositional clustering increases local cohesive energy and stabilizes the nanoparticle surface.
Uniform nanoparticles will exhibit surface disorder tens of degrees earlier than compositionally clustered nanoparticles.
The two nanoparticle populations may retain similar bulk melting temperatures despite different surface-premelting onsets.
The proposed effect should be observable when particle size and other processing parameters are controlled.
The effect is restricted to a temperature interval of roughly tens of degrees around the premelting onset.
Particle-size distribution and measurement resolution may influence the measured premelting-onset difference.
Statistically indistinguishable premelting onset temperatures and surface-disorder characteristics between the two populations would falsify the proposed governing role of atomic-level uniformity.

contradictions.description: The initial state calls a random atomic distribution 'atomic-scale configurational heterogeneity,' while the intervention classifies near-ideal random mixing as 'high atomic-level uniformity' and clustering as greater heterogeneity. The two fields therefore use uniformity and heterogeneity inconsistently.
